title: The rose-apple tree
hookLine: at the plowing festival the boy sits in the shade and falls into a quiet joy (MN 36)
last: SIDDHATTHA — A NAME IS A WISH.

cards: The plowing festival. The whole town is out in the fields: music, food, bright clothes, oxen with decorated horns, and the king himself takes hold of a golden plow to open the season. Everyone watches the king.
Nobody watches the boy. His nurses have set him down in the shade of a rose-apple tree at the edge of the field and wandered off to see the show. Alone, the boy sits cross-legged, quiet.
And something happens that he'll remember for the rest of his life.

teach.b: The festival details come from later tellings, but the heart of this story is the Buddha's own, from a discourse where he looks back on his search.
He's describing the punishing practices of those years, the fasting and the strain, and how they got him nowhere.

At his lowest point, he remembers: when his father was working in the fields, he sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree and entered a quiet joy, secluded from wanting, secluded from anything unwholesome, with a happiness born of that seclusion.

teach.h: THE FIRST JHANA: A QUIET JOY.
teach.b: He calls it the first jhana. Could that be the way to awakening? he wonders, and realizes it is.

teach.h: WHY AM I AFRAID OF THAT HAPPINESS?
teach.b: Then comes the question that turns his whole search around: why am I afraid of that kind of happiness, one that has nothing to do with the pleasures of the senses?
Jhana means deep meditative absorption: the mind settling, gathering, becoming still and bright. The texts describe four levels, each quieter than the last.
And a surprise: the Pali jhana is dhyana in Sanskrit. When Buddhism reached China, dhyana became chan. In Japan, chan became zen.
The name Zen comes from this word. For the Buddha, the point wasn't the joy itself.
It was the memory. Peace wasn't something he had to force, starve for or conquer. He'd found it by himself, as a child, doing nothing, in the shade.

how: Buddhists develop jhana through concentration meditation, often on the breath; it is taught in Theravada meditation traditions as the four absorptions, and the word itself, through Sanskrit dhyana and Chinese chan, gave Zen its name.

o: deep meditative absorption, still and bright
a trance where the mind goes fully blank
the moment of full awakening under the tree

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: where the boy found quiet joy

s: the rose-apple memory comes from the Buddha's own words in an old discourse
he recalls it in MN 36, while describing his hardships as a seeker.
the word Zen comes from jhana
jhana, dhyana, chan, zen: one word across four languages.
the Buddha decided the joy under the tree was dangerous
he asked: why am I afraid of that happiness? and saw it could be the way.

games.q: years later, starving and exhausted, the Buddha remembers the quiet joy under the rose-apple tree. what does he ask himself?
o: why can't I feel that anymore?
why am I afraid of that kind of happiness?
was it just a childhood dream?
games.why: why am I afraid of that happiness? it turns his search around: peace wasn't something to starve for. he'd found it before, as a child.

practice: If you can, sit somewhere shady: under a tree, by a window, in a quiet corner. Do nothing, not even meditating, exactly; be still the way a child is when nobody's watching, and let the breath do what it does.
If a little ease shows up, a small quiet pleasure in simply being here, don't be afraid of it: let it stay.

wordCard.voice: Jhana. Meditative absorption: the mind gathered, still and bright. Dhyana in Sanskrit, the root of chan and zen.

orig.note: Pali: meditative absorption. Sanskrit dhyāna, Chinese chan, Japanese zen.

carryVoice: Your line: you've been here before. Peace came first to a child in the shade. Day twenty-seven.
